photos.habitat: Freshwater lakes, ponds, and slow-moving rivers with vegetation across North America.
photos.funFact: Largemouth bass are ambush predators with excellent vision and can see in color. They can open their mouths wide enough to create a powerful suction that helps them capture prey.

photos.habitat: Cold, clear streams and lakes across North America and introduced worldwide.
photos.funFact: Rainbow trout can see ultraviolet light and have excellent color vision. They are known for their spectacular jumping ability when hooked or avoiding predators.

photos.habitat: Shallow, vegetated areas of lakes and slow rivers across northern regions.
photos.funFact: Northern pike are apex predators with razor-sharp teeth and can accelerate from 0 to 25 mph in seconds. They have been known to attack prey up to half their own size.

photos.habitat: Shallow waters of lakes, ponds, and slow streams with vegetation across North America.
photos.funFact: Male bluegills create circular nests in shallow water and aggressively defend them during breeding season. They can change color rapidly to communicate with other fish.

photos.habitat: Rivers, lakes, and ponds with muddy or sandy bottoms across North America.
photos.funFact: Channel catfish have over 100,000 taste buds covering their entire body, making them incredibly sensitive to chemical cues in the water. They can taste food before it enters their mouth.

photos.habitat: North Atlantic Ocean and rivers that flow into it for spawning.
photos.funFact: Atlantic salmon can jump up to 12 feet high to overcome waterfalls during their spawning migration. They return to the exact stream where they were born using their sense of smell.

photos.habitat: Cool lakes and rivers across northern North America.
photos.funFact: Walleyes have excellent night vision due to a reflective layer in their eyes called the tapetum lucidum. They are most active during dawn and dusk.

photos.habitat: Atlantic coast and connected rivers from Canada to Florida.
photos.funFact: Striped bass are anadromous, meaning they live in saltwater but spawn in freshwater. They can travel hundreds of miles during their seasonal migrations.

photos.habitat: Lakes, ponds, and slow rivers across northern North America.
photos.funFact: Yellow perch have excellent schooling behavior and can form groups of hundreds of individuals. Their distinctive yellow color with dark vertical bars makes them easy to identify.

photos.habitat: Large lakes and rivers in the Great Lakes region and eastern North America.
photos.funFact: Muskellunge are known as the 'fish of 10,000 casts' due to their elusive nature. They are the largest member of the pike family and can live over 30 years.

photos.habitat: Cold, clear streams and lakes in eastern North America.
photos.funFact: Brook trout are actually a type of char, not a true trout. They require very clean, cold water and are considered an indicator species for water quality.

photos.habitat: Rocky areas of lakes and rivers across North America.
photos.funFact: Smallmouth bass are known for their fighting ability and acrobatic jumps when hooked. They prefer cooler, clearer water than their largemouth cousins.

photos.habitat: Deep, cold lakes across northern North America.
photos.funFact: Lake trout can live over 40 years and grow to enormous sizes. They prefer deep, cold water and are often found at depths of 60-200 feet.

photos.habitat: Large lakes and rivers across central and eastern North America.
photos.funFact: White bass are highly social fish that travel in large schools. During spawning runs, thousands of fish can be seen moving up rivers together.

photos.habitat: Large, clear lakes with rocky or weedy areas in northern regions.
photos.funFact: Northern muskellunge are apex predators that can grow to massive sizes. They have been known to attack prey up to one-third their own body length.

photos.habitat: Pacific Ocean and tributaries from Alaska to California.
photos.funFact: Coho salmon undergo dramatic physical changes during spawning, with males developing hooked jaws and bright red coloration. They die after spawning, providing nutrients to forest ecosystems.

photos.habitat: Quiet waters of lakes, ponds, and slow rivers across North America.
photos.funFact: Crappies are excellent parents, with males building and guarding nests in shallow water. They can change color rapidly to blend with their surroundings.

photos.habitat: Shallow, weedy areas of lakes and ponds across North America.
photos.funFact: Sunfish are known for their bright colors and circular nests. Males become very territorial during breeding season and will attack anything that comes near their nest.

photos.habitat: Pacific Ocean from Alaska to California and their spawning rivers.
photos.funFact: Chinook salmon are the largest Pacific salmon species and can weigh over 100 pounds. They can travel over 2,000 miles from the ocean to their spawning grounds.

photos.habitat: Pacific Ocean and coastal rivers from Alaska to California.
photos.funFact: Steelhead are actually rainbow trout that migrate to the ocean. Unlike salmon, they can survive spawning and return to the ocean multiple times.

photos.habitat: Large rivers and reservoirs with deep pools across central North America.
photos.funFact: Flathead catfish are solitary predators that prefer live prey. They can grow to enormous sizes, with some specimens exceeding 100 pounds.

photos.habitat: Large rivers and lakes across northern North America.
photos.funFact: Saugers are closely related to walleyes but prefer flowing water. They have excellent low-light vision and are most active during twilight hours.

photos.habitat: Deep, cold lakes and rivers across northern regions.
photos.funFact: Burbot are the only freshwater member of the cod family. They spawn under ice in winter and are most active in cold water temperatures.

photos.habitat: Slow-moving rivers, lakes, and backwaters across eastern North America.
photos.funFact: Gar are living fossils that have remained virtually unchanged for 100 million years. They can breathe air and survive in low-oxygen water.

photos.habitat: Large rivers and reservoirs in the Mississippi River basin.
photos.funFact: Paddlefish are filter feeders with a distinctive paddle-shaped snout. They are one of the largest freshwater fish in North America and can live over 50 years.

photos.habitat: Shallow, vegetated waters of lakes and slow rivers in eastern North America.
photos.funFact: Bowfin are primitive fish that can breathe air and survive in low-oxygen water. Males guard their young in a nest and will aggressively defend them.

photos.habitat: Large rivers and lakes across central and eastern North America.
photos.funFact: Freshwater drum get their name from the drumming sound males make during spawning season. They are the only freshwater member of the drum family.

photos.habitat: Clear streams and rivers with rocky or sandy bottoms across North America.
photos.funFact: Redhorse suckers are bottom feeders that use their sucker-like mouths to feed on algae and small invertebrates. They play an important role in aquatic ecosystem health.

photos.habitat: Large rivers and lakes across central North America.
photos.funFact: Mooneyes have large, silvery eyes that reflect light, giving them their name. They are excellent jumpers and can leap several feet out of the water.

photos.habitat: Streams, rivers, and lakes across northern North America.
photos.funFact: White suckers are important forage fish for many predator species. They can tolerate a wide range of water conditions and are often the first fish to recolonize disturbed habitats.
